Cancer Crisis in KZN

By: Tarryn Crossman | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What is really happening in KZN to cause Oncologists to resign

Further information:
The saga with KZN DOH's oncology department started back in 2013 when CB did a story on the two Radiotherapy machines sitting dormant at Addington hospital. The contract for the maintenance of these machines was put into question and the department froze the payment to TecMed, the supplier in question. In 2015 the contract to maintain the Varian Radiotherapy machines was awarded to KZN oncology Inc., a company owned by Dr Zwane. There were multiple irregularities with this contract. The company KZN ocn Inc. was only registered after the minister announced that they had been awarded the contract. There was no tender published for this contract, the tender number on the contract was a for a cleaning service. Neither Dr Zwane or his third party supplier were certified by Varian to do maintenance on these radioactive machines, yet they have been paid are in writing the company responsible for maintaining these life saving machines.


Since March 2016 to today neither of these machines is working. In 6 months KZN has lost 6 oncologists, currently there are no oncologist at Addington or IALC, Grays has two left. Registers are running both these hospitals in DBN. There is a backlog of existing patients and currently no new patients are being accepted. So in theory there is nowhere in the whole of KZN, except Grays in Pietermaritzburg for cancer patients to go.

For years now the oncology department in KZN has been falling apart. Waiting periods from diagnoses to treatment have gone up from 4 week to anywhere between 6 months to a year, which is fatal for most cancer patients

As you will find out in two of our case studies

Gavins wife Celeste was 37 years old when she went into get a tumor removed from her throat, it was cancerous, but non of the radiotherapy machines at Addington or IALC and the waiting list at Grays was 6 months, she didn’t have that much time. Her oncologist sent her to Bloemfontein to try and get treatment, but they denied her treatment, as she was not from the province. Even though she had a referral letter begging them to treat her. She returned to KZN and waited 6 more weeks, eventually she managed to get an appointment for chemo. At this stage another tumor was starting to grow out of the cut where her previous tumor was removed. By the time the radiography machine starting working it was too late for Celeste. She passed away in November 2016, leaving behind her husband and two children

Pamela’s mother was in pain and bleeding for weeks, but she couldn’t get an appointment at Northdale, so her daughter eventually took her to a private GP, where the GP battled to even get a pap smear as her cervix was bleeding so much. He immediately said it seems like cancer and she need to see an oncologist
In January 2016 they did a biopsy on her at Northdale and one month later the results came back positive. When she went to Grays to try and get an appointment they said she would have to wait until September 7 months just to see an oncologist. They knew someone who worked at Grays and managed to convince her to illegally get Pamela’s mom an appointment for March
When went in the doctor said she will have to start Chemo in April and sent her home. When she returned to start her Chemo, he said it was too late and that the cancer had spread to her liver and lungs. She died on the 21st April

Geraldine in 27 she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer and sold her car to go and get private care at Victoria hospital, they did had a hysterectomy and prescribed immediate radio therapy. This was in October 2016; 9 months later Geraldine is still waiting for her appointment, which is due on the 27th of June. But with no oncologists left she is not sure what will happen next. In good medical practice Geraldine should have had the radiotherapy no later that 4 weeks post surgery. Essentially this waiting period has made her surgery nil and void

Press Release:


KZN Oncology
In recent weeks, the KZN public health sector has come under scrutiny after one of the last State oncologists resigned. Now without specialists, several broken
radiotherapy machines and long waiting lists for emergency procedures, cancer patients remain untreated. Carte Blanche finds out what’s really behind the province’s
oncology crisis.

2 00:14 Kate My mother was diagnosed February 2017 and up until April 2017 we had received no treatment
3 00:23 Devi introduction The KZN oncology unit is in crises. There are only two oncologist and 3 radiotherapy machines to service an entire province resulting in massive treatment backlog

5 01:00 Interview with Tseliso Thipanyane Tseliso: There are basically 3 public hospitals in the province, which provide for the oncology issues. With the two hospitals Addington and Albert Luthuli hospital at this point in time all the oncologist resigned because of the challenges related to working conditions in the hospital.
6 01:19 Voice over Grey’s state hospital in Pietermaritzburg has the only two oncologists serving the whole province. There are 5 radiotherapy machines in KZN, one is at Greys, two are at Albert Luthuli and the other two are at Addington and have not been fully functional since 2009
7 01:25 Devi interview with Tseliso Thipanyane
Devi: in the end this is a matter of life and death
Tseliso: this is a matter of life and death that’s why we are asking the department to tell us how many patients have died because of the inability to do their jobs

9 01:58 Devi link Tumour were removed from her neck and tongue, she was given a good prognosis provided she started radiation immediately after surgery
10 02:09 Gavin interview Gavin: we got a referral to go to Albert Luthuli because she had no medical aid. And I think half the country doesn’t have medical aid because of the price and the costs. 11 02:37 Devi link Kate has asked us to hide her identity her mom passed away from cervical cancer after waiting for months and never receiving treatment
12 02:45 Kate interview kATE: we got the results of the biopsy on the 9th of February and they confirmed that my mom did have cancer and it was cervical cancer which was 5mm, stage 2 is treatable. 13 03:18 Voice over for Geraldine and family Geraldine was first diagnosed with a malignant tumor in her ovary in October 2016. 14 03:42 Geraldine Geraldine: when I went Albert Luthuli uhm not a lot happened. The explanation given by the department back then was procurement issues. MEC Dlomo was the MEC when these problems all started.
16 04:23 Interview with MEC Dr. Dhlomo: In 2009 the machines were procured thought a company called Tech Med, suddenly Tech Med says no we don't have a maintenance contract we have to pay for this separately

Devi: you mean it took 2 years to do something about it
Mec: that is why there was an involvemnet of the mother company called Varian
Devi: But when did varian come in to do the job?
Mec: they’ve just started now.
Devi: now?
Mec: we spoke to them in 2012
Deviu: but nobody was fixing the macines MEC
MEC: they were being fixed on and off

MEC: In retrospect everybody says that
Devi: so at the moment who has the contract to maintain those machines

25 07:41 Geraldine: well within a month it grew from 4,6 cm to 12,7cm

27 08:10 Geraldine: I just feel like I'm another number

29 08:16 Interview with Devi and MEC Devi; so who's fault is this?
MEC: Who's fault is what?
Devi: what? the oncology crisis in KZN who's fault is it?
MEC: It depends you have a different view and I have a different view.
Devi: what is your view?
MEC: the point of our fault is that it lies with the person who never fixed the machines
Devi: are you passing the bar MEC?
MEC: I don’t fix machines
Devi: yes but you are responsible and you’re the MEC of Health
MEC: that is why I say me and you will have a different view point on this matter.
Devi: what would you like say to the families that have lost loved ones? Waiting for chemo therapy, waiting for radiation? What would you like to say?
MEC: No I will talk to them and not you I will find space because I’m working that with the human rights commission process with them


30 09:08 Tseliso Thipanyane
Well the constitution very clear that the MEC and his people must take reasonable measures and if they take reasonable measures to address this problem I don't think we would be where we are today. Its high time that we make sure that those who cost deaths in this country due to the failure to do their jobs or to uphold the constitution pay for it.

Waiting periods from diagnoses to treatment have gone up from 4 week to anywhere between 6 months to a year, which is fatal for most cancer patients As you will find out in two of our case studies Gavins wife Celeste was 37 years old when she went into get a tumor removed from her throat, it was cancerous, but non of the radiotherapy machines at Addington or IALC and the waiting list at Grays was 6 months, she didn’t have that much time. Her oncologist sent her to Bloemfontein to try and get treatment, but they denied her treatment, as she was not from the province. Even though she had a referral letter begging them to treat her. She returned to KZN and waited 6 more weeks, eventually she managed to get an appointment for chemo. At this stage another tumor was starting to grow out of the cut where her previous tumor was removed. By the time the radiography machine starting working it was too late for Celeste. She passed away in November 2016, leaving behind her husband and two children Pamela’s mother was in pain and bleeding for weeks, but she couldn’t get an appointment at Northdale, so her daughter eventually took her to a private GP, where the GP battled to even get a pap smear as her cervix was bleeding so much. He immediately said it seems like cancer and she need to see an oncologist In January 2016 they did a biopsy on her at Northdale and one month later the results came back positive. When she went to Grays to try and get an appointment they said she would have to wait until September 7 months just to see an oncologist. They knew someone who worked at Grays and managed to convince her to illegally get Pamela’s mom an appointment for March When went in the doctor said she will have to start Chemo in April and sent her home. When she returned to start her Chemo, he said it was too late and that the cancer had spread to her liver and lungs. She died on the 21st April Geraldine in 27 she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer and sold her car to go and get private care at Victoria hospital, they did had a hysterectomy and prescribed immediate radio therapy. This was in October 2016; 9 months later Geraldine is still waiting for her appointment, which is due on the 27th of June. But with no oncologists left she is not sure what will happen next. In good medical practice Geraldine should have had the radiotherapy no later that 4 weeks post surgery. Essentially this waiting period has made her surgery nil and void
